name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s ‘unprecedented’ budget vote leaves schools around Kansas City in the lurch
description: School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year. The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, [[...]
text:
A student at Ingels Elementary School in the Hickman Mills School District. Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the Missouri State Board of Education’s decision not to request full funding for schools (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year.
The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, especially when money is tight. The most recent statewide school budget fell $190 million short.
Still, some local and statewide education leaders were caught off guard when the Missouri State Board of Education at its Sept. 15 meeting approved a budget request that didn’t even ask for the full amount required to fund the formula.
They said the decision is unprecedented, to their knowledge, and undersells how much money schools need according to the framework that the legislature itself created. 
Instead, the state school board’s request asks the governor and the legislature to keep foundation formula funding flat compared to the current year’s already underfunded budget. That means that in the coming fiscal year, state school funding would fall more than $270 million under what is laid out in state law. 
Hickman Mills Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the board’s decision, suggesting the move gives lawmakers an easy pass to continue depriving Missouri schools of deeply needed resources.
It “makes it more likely that we’ll get less than we received last year, because we remove the ability to have a strong conversation about the foundation formula not simply being something that’s on a spreadsheet,” he said. “It represents what the state determined was necessary to effectively educate children.”
The latest decision is just one way school funding is “under assault” at the local, state and federal levels, Carpenter said.
Jackson County schools are preparing for property tax refunds to cut millions of dollars out of their budgets, and schools have seen federal funding delayed, cut or threatened.
“We keep asking the system to do more with less,” Carpenter said. “At some point, the system can’t function at a level that we all can be proud of.”
 The board’s discussion

The decision came after the state board voted 4-4 on a budget recommendation that did include full foundation formula funding. The tie meant the proposal did not pass.
Democrats Jordan Bradberry and Vincent Schoemehl Jr., Republican Kerry Casey and Jon Otto, an independent, voted in favor of full funding. Republicans Kenneth “Brooks” Miller Jr., Michael Matousek and Robbie Myers, along with independent Gretchen Shull, voted no.
The board also has a new nonvoting member, Mike McDonald, who is a math teacher in the Park Hill School District.
Board members are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Missouri Senate. Their political affiliations are reported because no more than four may belong to the same party.
Matousek, a member from Kansas City, called for the board to disregard the funding formula, arguing that the department shouldn’t request a funding increase at all while it lacks a strategic plan and a permanent commissioner.
“I think we’re asking for a lot of money without a real justification for spending it,” he said.
“This board, this department, has a credibility problem, and I think sending over a nine-plus billion dollar budget to people who make these decisions doesn’t help.”
He said that while state law requires the department to calculate the full foundation formula amount, it doesn’t require that the budget request match.
“I think we’re asking for money that doesn’t exist,” he said, alluding to a tightening state budget.
In June, Missouri Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick warned that the state’s general revenue surplus is being depleted.
Casey said it isn’t the board’s role to determine whether funding is available. That’s the responsibility of the state’s legislative and executive branches.
“It’s our job to present the need,” she said. The governor and legislature “are the ones to determine how that works in the scheme of all of the bigger priorities within the budget. That is not our job.”
After the tie vote, the board reached a compromise to leave in budget requests tied to new initiatives ordered by Gov. Mike Kehoe, the legislature or the courts. Those include a plan to grade public schools and districts on an A-to-F scale, new antisemitism reporting requirements and increased oversight of athletics.
It approved a nearly $4.3 billion request for the foundation formula, the same as formula spending in fiscal year 2027. That’s $270 million less than full funding for the formula.
McDonald clarified that the only change from the budget the board voted down was a cut to school budgets.
“I guess my concern is that the easiest place to cut is from the funding of the districts,” he said.
 Local impact

Carpenter, whose south Kansas City district is digging itself out of a financial hole and fighting to earn full accreditation, said it’s striking that the board voted to underfund schools shortly after approving a framework to grade them on an A-to-F scale.
“I think it’s pretty interesting that we literally up the ante on accountability,” he said, “and we reduce the ante on the resources necessary to be successful.”
The foundation formula isn’t just his personal opinion about how much schools should receive, Carpenter said. “The state made that determination, and now we’ve gotten so comfortable with underfunding it that we’re now comfortable for not even asking for full funding.”
In the Lee’s Summit School District, about 28% of funding comes from the state, said Chad Hertzog, assistant superintendent of business services. 
When state funding lags, the district has to rely even more on local funding, he said, including potentially raising residents’ property taxes. Once the district hits the tax rate ceiling set by voters, it has to reduce expenses such as by cutting supplies, services and staff.
The district could also ask taxpayers to raise the tax ceiling.
“It’s not (an option) that we like to consider because again, we’re asking our local voters to ultimately fund shortfalls at the state level at even a higher rate than they already are,” he said.
Hertzog said the district’s most pressing problem is Jackson County property taxes, but state funding reductions add to budget concerns. KCUR reports that the district is anticipating a revenue reduction of $7 million to $10 million this year after it reduced the tax rate in 2023 in response to growing property assessments.
The county has since determined that those assessments were handled incorrectly and is planning to refund money to taxpayers, cutting into schools’ revenue.
Hertzog said the difference between full formula funding from the state and what the district is actually receiving is nearly $7 million. The district’s overall operating budget is more than $280 million.
Carter Taylor, a Kansas City Public Schools elementary teacher and legislative chair of the Kansas City Federation of Teachers union, said the state board’s decision felt in line with “the current era in Missouri politics.”
“This is just another move that says public education doesn’t deserve support or funding,” she said. “It is another not-so-subtle attempt to say that we shouldn’t really exist.”
School districts’ percentage of state funding varies widely depending on factors such as the value of property that can be taxed locally. KCPS is one district that receives relatively little from the state, but Taylor said that every dollar counts.
“We take the least, and we try so hard to put in the most, but there’s only so much that a good teacher can do,” she said.
Matt Michelson, director of education policy for the Missouri State Teachers Association, said that even flat funding represents a practical decrease for schools as costs rise.
“I think all of us see in our daily lives everything is getting more expensive,” he said. Schools are “not immune to those increases in costs that everyone’s experienced over the last year,” including raises for teachers who also experience the effects of inflation.
Sarah Laub, a parent of two in the Blue Springs School District, said she’s concerned that state funding decisions could lead to her kids losing teachers and extracurricular activities. She’s also worried rural school districts — like the one she left in search of more educational opportunities for her kids in a better-funded district — could be hit the hardest.
Laub was referred to The Beacon by the Will of the People PAC, which aims to flip Missouri legislative seats. She also worked to oppose Amendment 5 with Parents for Missouri Public Schools based on its predicted impact on school funding.
She said the board’s decision should be seen in the context of a political climate where Kehoe and the legislature haven’t supported full school funding.
“It sounds like the board made their decision to not request that funding, not based on the belief that the schools don’t need it, but instead based on the belief that they no longer have faith that the lawmakers would listen to them or provide it,” she said.
But she thinks the board’s decision could contribute to lower school funding.
“I am concerned that this has created a vicious cycle where now the legislature will use it as a reason to cut even more funds,” she said.
 The message to lawmakers and the public

Lindsey Baker, research director with the Missouri Budget Project, a center-left think tank, said there are plenty of historical examples of fully funding the state’s formula and the lack of full funding. But whatever the ultimate outcome, the education department always requested full funding from lawmakers.
“This is not something I have ever seen, certainly, and I’ve talked to many other people who have been around a lot longer than I have, who have never seen this before either,” Baker said.
“I think this is an indication that this is going to be a very painful budget year.”
Baker attributed state budget issues to years of tax cuts that she said have caused a “serious revenue problem.”
The board’s decision could have a mixed reception in the legislature, said Caitlin Whaley, senior director of advocacy for the Missouri School Boards’ Association (MSBA). Those against higher school funding might use it to their advantage, while others won’t be pleased.
“It certainly gives legislators something to hang their hat on if they can say, ‘Well, why should we fully fund it if the very board that we confirmed to oversee public education doesn’t think this funding is necessary?’” she said.
But “there are absolutely supporters of public education in the legislature,” she said, “that will now have a decidedly more negative view of the state board.”
Whaley said lawmakers shouldn’t be surprised by increased costs because the legislature had projections of the financial impact when they voted on the changes that have caused some of the increases to the foundation formula. Those changes include incentives for five-day school weeks and relying less on attendance when computing enrollment for funding purposes.
Attendance-based calculations of enrollment tend to penalize schools that have higher poverty rates.
A task force is working on a proposal to modernize Missouri’s school funding formula, which could further increase the cost of the formula.
Whaley said that as the budget process continues, MSBA will highlight stories of school districts that are facing budget challenges and emphasize that the state should fulfill its commitments.
“If we’re going to pass legislation that says we’re going to pay districts money, that we need to, as a state, be responsible for those decisions that are made,” she said.
In an emailed news release, Missouri Association of School Administrators Executive Director Mark Penny also criticized the board decision.
“This is a failure of the board’s most basic responsibility: advocating for Missouri’s public schools and the students they serve,” the statement read in part. “The board’s job is to tell the governor and the General Assembly what our schools need. Instead, this board has made the unprecedented choice to recommend that public schools remain underfunded, an action that reflects a board increasingly hostile to public education.”
Michelson said he’s not sure how legislators will respond, but he sees the recommendation as a poor start to the budget process.
“It sends a horrible message to our educators, our kids and our communities that the state board doesn’t believe that it’s necessary to even ask the legislature to fully fund our schools,” Michelson said.
This article first appeared on Beacon: Kansas City and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee schools still miss farm-to-school grant eliminated in 2025 as USDA rolls out new programs
description: School Nutrition Director Vickie Dunaway has spent years transitioning the Milan Special School District in West Tennessee toward scratch-made cooking. She used grant funding to purchase equipment needed to process whole foods in school kitchens, and she bought fresh corn, squash, tomatoes and local beef from farmers for student meals. But in March 2025, the[...]
text:
Tennessee schools are still feeling the loss of Local Foods for Schools funding eliminated by the Trump administration in 2025. The U.S. Department of agriculture recently announced a new 'Harvest to Hallways' initiative, which offers guidance and funding for equipment, among other things. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)School Nutrition Director Vickie Dunaway has spent years transitioning the Milan Special School District in West Tennessee toward scratch-made cooking.
She used grant funding to purchase equipment needed to process whole foods in school kitchens, and she bought fresh corn, squash, tomatoes and local beef from farmers for student meals.
But in March 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture canceled the Local Food for Schools program that helped her district afford fresh local foods — more expensive than pre-processed commodities — amid the Trump administration’s efforts to slash the federal budget. 
“We were able to chop the tomatoes and shred the lettuce and all the squash and sweet potatoes and all the things,” Dunaway said. “We bought the equipment. Now I can’t afford the food.”
The U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Department of Health and Human Services announced a new slate of programs in late August aiming to bring more American agriculture products to school cafeteria trays. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The “Harvest to Hallways” initiative includes up to $70 million for schools to update cafeteria equipment and storage, and an additional $25 million infusion into Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grants, which support projects that connect schools with local producers. The USDA will also offer guidance to schools looking to use their existing school lunch federal reimbursement dollars on local foods. Another $32.5 million HHS program will help school districts test new approaches.
Dunaway said it’s a step in the right direction: Many schools need help building the infrastructure to handle fresh foods, and the local option for reimbursement dollars is helpful. But these things don’t change her budget’s bottom line. 
“We need both the equipment to process the fresh ingredients (and) a sustainable recurring revenue that helps make buying food possible long-term,” she said.
The USDA has yet to publish application requirements for the new grants. The Tennessee Department of Education is awaiting guidance from the USDA, Director of Media Amanda Chin said in an email to The Lookout.
If any of the opportunities provide funding to help purchase fresh, local food, Dunaway said she’ll be “the first one jumping in.”
Otherwise, she’d rather have the money go to schools that don’t already have the necessary equipment, she said. But that may also be difficult.
“For so many of us, writing that grant and staying on top of that grant is not something that a lot of the small districts can do,” Dunaway said. “They just don’t have the staff, and they don’t have the time to do all that.”
Grant-funded program to bring cooking labs, fresh local foods to Northwest Tennessee schools

The nonprofit Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network secured a $500,000 Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grant this year and is working with five school districts over the next two years to train cafeteria workers to work with fresh produce and introduce new foods to students. Dunaway’s school district is among those benefiting from that program.
The nonprofit’s co-directors Samantha Smith Goyret and Caroline Ideus said they are grateful to see the administration’s focus moving toward supporting more local ingredients in school meals but noted the federal grant process may be a challenge for smaller, less-resourced schools and organizations to tackle without experience.
“We worked with several smaller school districts to help write Farm to School grants this past cycle, but they weren’t awarded because they’re not strong enough, they’re not big enough,” Smith Goyret said. “So what the government is doing, it’s really fueling the organizations that already have that capacity.”
Barriers to offering more local food in schools boil down to three points: education, equipment and lack of funding, Smith Goyret said. The recently announced grants could help reduce some of those barriers, she said.
But the loss of the Local Food for Schools funding in 2025 “was a huge blow and still is,” Ideus said.
The program, which started during the COVID-19 pandemic, earmarked about $660 million for schools and childcare institutions to purchase locally produced foods in 2025 under outgoing President Joe Biden’s administration. Another $500 million was earmarked for local food purchases for food banks.
“That was a direct pipeline to the schools for them to use for local food, period,” Ideus said. “So these grants that they’re dibbling out are nice, but it’s not $1 billion.”
Having both the Farm to School grants and the Local Food for Schools funding would be the “ultimate” combination, she said.
Schools get reimbursed a set amount by the federal government for eligible meals and snacks they serve, but the budget is tight, and local foods can be considerably more expensive than commodity products, Smith Goyret said.
“Even wholesale, farmers still have to make ends meet. They’re not charitable organizations. They’re businesses as well,” she said.
Dunaway said the cost of even commodity foods is rising, but local farming operations can’t compete with bulk prices. Now, she’s only able to purchase sausage and beef from a local source “on special occasions.”
A spokesperson for the USDA pointed to USDA Foods, a program that allows schools to use preset federal entitlements to order domestically produced fruits, vegetables, meat and other foods procured by the USDA and delivered through a partnership with the Department of Defense’s logistics agency. The spokesperson also highlighted $45 million issued in 2026 through Farm to School grants, in addition to other programs that distribute locally sourced foods to tribal members.
In 2023, nearly two-thirds of school food authorities reported serving local foods to students, according to the USDA’s 2023 Farm to School Census. Those districts logged nearly $1.8 billion in local food purchases, about 16% of total spending. About half of that went toward local milk. That year, 42% of participating school food authorities reported challenges with availability of local foods, and 35% reported cost difficulties.
The next Farm to School Census is slated for 2027, according to a USDA spokesperson.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Could Virginia’s new law allowing 1% sales tax for school construction need a fix?
description: A new state law allowing localities to raise revenue for school construction has opened opportunities but also raised questions, with some local leaders and lawmakers asking if it could create funding shortfalls for localities that approve the measure. Virginia voters to decide on 1% sales tax for school construction, NoVa transit funding Right before the […[...]
text:
The historic facade of Virginia's new General Assembly Building in Richmond. (Photo by Sarah Vogelsong/Virginia Mercury)A new state law allowing localities to raise revenue for school construction has opened opportunities but also raised questions, with some local leaders and lawmakers asking if it could create funding shortfalls for localities that approve the measure.
Virginia voters to decide on 1% sales tax for school construction, NoVa transit funding

Right before the July 1 deadline, Virginia passed a budget that included language allowing localities, pending voter support, to raise a 1% sales tax primarily to cover school construction due to unprecedented costs. 
The revenue could also cover public transportation needs in Planning District 8, which includes localities in Northern Virginia. 
The tax cap will last for 20 years after local leaders pass a resolution. The resolution must specify the tax’s expiration date or, if the projects are financed through bonds or loans, when the borrower must repay those obligations. This can make the timeline harder to manage when financing happens later.
Since bonds may not be acquired until much later but the 20-year countdown starts immediately when the measure is approved, localities may have a tougher time providing a predictable, long-term revenue stream that matches the life, financing and capital needs of school facilities.
“We want this to be an effective tool for localities for rebuilding crumbling school infrastructure across the commonwealth, and if we need to look at that sunset provision so that it’s more usable, I think we should do it,” House Education Committee Vice Chair Del. Shelly Simonds told The Mercury in a recent interview. 
Simonds raised the matter at the state’s Sept. 8 commission meeting on School Construction in Modernization, the first meeting since the group met in December 2022. Her comments followed a presentation on the 1% sales tax and the potential impact on localities.
After speaking with Newport News officials in the district she represents, she said they expressed concern that the bill’s expiration of the government’s power to impose the tax may not line up with the timeline needed to issue bonds against that revenue stream — something the delegate had not heard about before the city raised it.
Still, Simonds said the city is excited about the new tax option for school construction because it could help address multiple deteriorating school buildings needing replacement. 
“We know that we’ve got roofs and HVACs that need to be replaced, but there are other things that we need in today’s modern school building,” Simonds said. “Just think about the technology needs that our schools have now: high-speed internet, fiber-optic networks. There’s a lot to consider beyond just the brick-and-mortar traditional school building.” 
House Education Committee Chair Sam Rasoul, D-Roanoke, who carried legislation in the past to provide the sales tax option for localities, told the Mercury he’s “committed to giving our local schools all the tools and support we can to help with school construction needs, which includes more flexibility.”
After speaking with Newport News officials in the district she represents, Simonds said they expressed concern that the bill’s temporary power to impose the tax may not line up with the timeline needed to issue bonds against that revenue stream.
Simonds said she had not heard about that issue before the city raised it. Newport News is one of 47 localities seeking voter support in November to implement the tax.
Simonds said she and her colleagues will wait to hear what experts have to say at a future meeting.
Del. Chris Runion, R-Rockingham, also requested additional information at a future meeting on whether the sales tax revenue could be used for regional Career and Technical Education centers, existing bond payments, and construction already underway. The final budget excluded those provisions.
“I think if we’re interested in making the localities remove some of the fiscal stress from them, so they can provide this high-quality education that we’re demanding from them, I think it makes sense, and I would encourage us to readdress that issue,” Runion said.
Both matters center on the mismatch between when the money is available and when localities actually need it.
The commission requested a presentation on procurement and bonding at a future, unscheduled meeting.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Middleton referendum discussion highlights tension between property taxes and school funding
description: Kate Murrain, a realtor and mother of two Middleton-Cross Plains School District students, said she has a couple of questions before she makes her mind up whether to vote for the district’s $118.5 million referendum request.  Murrain told the Wisconsin Examiner that she wants to see a side-by-side comparison of budgets, one of if the […]
text:
Bob Hesselbein and Middleton community members discuss the upcoming school referendum request that will appear on ballots. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Kate Murrain, a realtor and mother of two Middleton-Cross Plains School District students, said she has a couple of questions before she makes her mind up whether to vote for the district’s $118.5 million referendum request. 
Murrain told the Wisconsin Examiner that she wants to see a side-by-side comparison of budgets, one of if the referendum passes and one if it fails. Her questions reflect the competing concerns that surfaced in a recent public discussion of rising property taxes and the school district’s troubles meeting rising costs. 
“At this point, without any information and being as educated as I need to be I would vote no,” Murrain said, adding she noticed that the meeting was attended by a relatively small group of neighbors who appeared to be pro-referendum. “I was surprised. I expected to walk into 100 people having questions to get better educated. I’m just shocked that this is the turnout.”
Murrain was one of about 20 who gathered in the performing arts center of Middleton High School on Sept. 17 to listen to district leaders explain the request and take questions. The district is holding at least four of these sessions open to the public leading up to the Nov. 3 election.
Middleton’s request is part of a wave of more than 70 school district referendum requests this fall seeking $1.6 billion in support from property taxpayers. Under Wisconsin’s school funding system, there is a cap on how much school districts can bring in through a combination of state aid and property taxes. To exceed the caps, Wisconsin school districts have to go to voters for approval. 
Among the requests 17 are for one-time building costs, eight are recurring, to provide permanent support for operating costs, and the remaining are non-recurring, slated to help with operating costs but for a set number of years.
By the end of the year, the total number of referendum requests appearing on spring and fall ballots will total more than 150. Eight of the school districts asking voters for more money in November are trying for the second time this year after a spring request failed. 
In April, 75 referendum requests went before voters. According to the Wisconsin Policy Forum, 46 of those passed — a 61.3% approval rate. The Policy Forum found that a similar result in November would represent “a substantial decrease from the 70.1% approval rate in 2024” and the “lowest approval rate of any even-numbered year since 2010, when voters approved 52.7% of referenda.”
The Middleton-Cross Plains School District request is the second largest referendum ask  on ballots in November behind Green Bay Area School District, which is seeking $158 million over four years and is currently a party in a lawsuit suing the state over the school funding formula.
Middleton is considered “property rich,” meaning it gets less state aid than other school districts and relies more heavily on property taxes for its budget. According to school leaders, about 80% of the district budget comes from property taxes. The other 20% comes from state aid. 
The request would be split to provide $24.9 million in year one of the referendum. That amount would continue the funding the district is currently receiving through a 2022 nonrecurring referendum. The next three years the funding would rise by about 3% each year to account for inflation, so $27.9 million in year two, $31.1 million in year three and $34.6 million in year four.
Bob Hesselbein, the school board president, told the Examiner that the district considered about six different referendum scenarios.
“Like a lot of districts within Wisconsin since 2010, we have been forced to find operational funding with our own community because the state each year is giving us in real dollars less in buying power,” Hesselbein said. “We recognize with the economics going on now in the country, we didn’t want to ask for more because everyone’s hurting.”
The district conducted surveys while working to develop the question. In one survey of about 1,800 community members, 66% said that they would probably or definitely vote for a 2026 referendum. Those who opposed the referendum cited property-tax fatigue, spending reductions and a preference for state level solutions. 
Hesselbein said the district hasn’t had a “No Vote” committee form. In other districts, “No Vote” and “Yes Vote” committees will form and can come into contention with one another as residents concerned about rising property taxes are pitted against those who want their schools to be able to meet costs.
One attendee at the recent meeting in Middleton asked for clarification on the actual cost to individual taxpayers of the referendum and said he was worried about how the additional taxes would affect seniors on a fixed income.
An explanatory page provided by the district shows that property taxpayers could expect to pay no additional money in the first year, $21 in the second, $40 in the third and $59 in the fourth. However, the numbers are pegged to $100,000 of property. The district said it provided the information in the form it did so individuals could do the math easily depending on the cost of the house. 
“Who has a $100,000 house in Middleton?” the attendee said. “I’d rather see the average house in there, so people can get a feel as to what you’re looking at.” 
The average cost of a house is $500,000 in Middleton, meaning in the second year of the budget an average homeowner could expect to pay an additional $105 in property taxes in the second year of the referendum.
“You’re going to be squeezing me,” the attendee said. “You want to keep everything status quo. There’s room to cut.” 
If the referendum fails the district will have to cut its budget by about 20%. 
Whether the referendum passes or not, the district plans to cut $5 million from its budget, though conversations are just beginning on where those cuts will come from. 
“We’re going to probably find ourselves cutting some of the enhancements to education, not the meat of what we do here,” Hesselbein told the Examiner, adding that it likely wouldn’t mean layoffs, but retirements may mean conversations about dividing work among current employees instead of a new hire. 
The same retiree who spoke up about the cost of the referendum asked why the district wasn’t turning to state lawmakers. 
“I called Sen. [Dianne] Hesselbein’s office last year, and asked, what have you done to get more money?” he said. “I got the typical political run around.”
Gov. Tony Evers and Republican lawmakers tried to pass a deal earlier this year that would have tapped the state surplus to give schools some additional funding and send rebate checks to property taxpayers. The bill failed in the Senate, where most Democrats opposed it, saying it didn’t do enough to help schools or spend money responsibly, along with a couple of Republicans, who opposed the spending. 
Since then, progress on school funding changes have been stalled as most politicians have turned their attention to the upcoming elections. 
Bob Hesselbein, who is married to the Democratic leader of the Senate, said he had some inside information for the disgruntled taxpayer at the Middleton meeting.
“I happen to know Sen. Hesselbein pretty well,” he said, drawing a few chuckles in the room. 
“You can yell and swear all you want,” he added. “In Dane County, we have very pro-education representation in both our Assembly and our Senate. Unfortunately, they’re a minority within the state of Wisconsin, and until the rest of the cities, Wisconsin, come to that realization that their public schools are being damaged, we can’t expect anything different from our local politicians, because that’s the constitutional laws of our state.”
Sen. Hesselbein has said that Democrats will pass legislation to fund public schools in January. 
“We are going to be fully there for our public schools, especially when it comes to special education reimbursement,” Sen. Dianne Hesselbein said at a press conference last week. “One thing that school administrators are telling us all across the state — principals as well — that they want to see something they can count on and they want to rely on it.” 
Sen. Hesselbein said that her caucus has started having conversations over the summer about what needs to happen, including putting more money into special education and general aid. She said Democrats are also looking at other states to understand how the school funding formula could be changed.
“We’re also looking at a long-term goal of seeing what other states are doing and how they are funding their public schools, but that’s going to take probably a multi-year task to try to figure that all out and talking to our friends in Minnesota, Michigan, Illinois,” Hesselbein said. 
Meanwhile, school districts continue to rely on taxpayers to help them meet costs. 
Jim Coursey, treasurer of the Middleton school board, explained the stakes to Murrain. 
“If we were to lose that 20% of the budget, there will be no question that classrooms will be impacted, that’s too much,” Coursey said. “That’s going to lead to larger class sizes because it’s going to lead to a reduction in the number of staff that we’re going to be able to have supporting. It’s going to lead to elimination of programs.” 
Murrain, who said she values the education her children are receiving, remained unconvinced.
“I don’t know, it’s tough… I would need to see exactly where those funds are being allocated,” she said.
